item.title: Let all children be children
item.description:
Since May 2026, Bangladesh has witnessed repeated cases of child sexual abuse and child murder following sexual assault Protests erupted. Social media filled with grief and rage. People demanded justice. Yet the cases have not stopped. On 26 September 2026, another case was reported.
The outrage followed again. But between the anger, a familiar thread appears: some people still blame the children. They ask what the child was wearing, where she went, why she was alone. Such comments reveal something just as dangerous, a permission structure that treats some children as fair game.
According to Bangladesh Mahila Parishad, 543 children were victims of sexual abuse in 2025 alone. Many organisations, including UNICEF, warn that the real number is higher, because most victims never come forward.
Many adolescents are groomed, manipulated, and sexually abused by predatory adults who hide exploitation behind the curtain of romance.
Shockingly, a large part of society seems willing to accept that form of abuse. But is it really shocking? In the past, child marriage was widely accepted in Bangladesh. In the 2000s, 27% of girls were married by the age of 16. The law has changed.
The trend may have declined. But, has the mindset really changed?
The practice may have died down, but the mindset has not vanished. It hides behind polite smiles and surfaces when people feel comfortable enough to blame a child. Look again at the comments that blame victims.
Do those commenters see a child?
Or do they see someone who was "old enough," "mature enough," or "asking for it"?
These are the same excuses used to justify child marriage, to silence survivors, and to protect abusers.
"She is mature for her age."
"She looks old."
"She dresses up a lot."
"She goes out a lot."
"She posts a lot of photos."
These excuses are portable. If they work for a 16-year-old, they can be stretched to a 14-year-old. If they work for a 14-year-old, they can be stretched to a 12-year-old. Then to a 9-year-old. The age changes; the logic does not. This does not mean that every person who abuses a teenager will go on to abuse a younger child. It is a claim about the permission structure we allow to circulate.
Once we accept that a child can be blamed for her own abuse, we have already accepted the core idea that makes all child sexual abuse easier to excuse.
The line keeps moving. That is the danger.
Many girls in Bangladesh still grow up hearing that they must change how they sit, speak, dress, or move, or they will not find a husband. This is often masked under humour. But it is not funny. It teaches a girl that her body exists for marriage and male approval before she can understand what either means.
It tells her that her safety is her responsibility, not the adult's. And it tells abusers that society may take their side.
Children's and adolescents' brains are still developing. They cannot legally consent. Teenagers are not adults simply because they look older or because an adult finds them attractive.
Under the law, a child is a child. The age of consent and child marriage laws exist precisely because adults are responsible for not exploiting young people's vulnerability.
Yet society often draws an arbitrary line: "Younger children are victims, but teenagers are somehow complicit."
Why?
There is no age limit for victim-blaming.
If a 15-year-old is told she was mature, then a 12-year-old is told she dressed older. Then a 7-year-old is told she should have known better. If we truly saw all children as children, it would be much harder to see them as something else.
The solution is not only punishment after the fact but also prevention. Educating and refusing to stay silent is the best way to start.
We must believe children when they speak up. We must stop questioning what they did wrong.
We must hold accountable the relatives, neighbours, and online commenters who blame victims. We must enforce child marriage and sexual abuse laws again and again, regardless of the abuser's status.
We must teach young boys that girls' bodies are not theirs to comment on, touch, or control. We must teach girls that they are not responsible for the violence of adults. We must support survivors with counselling, legal aid, and safe spaces. And we must stop treating teenagers as a separate, disposable category of children.
Children are the most precious and vulnerable part of humanity.
It is our duty as humans to keep them safe. That duty does not expire when a child turns 13 or 16.
It does not weaken because a girl "looks older" or because she is outgoing.
Every child deserves protection. Every child deserves justice. Every child deserves to be seen as a child.
Let all children be children.
Humayra Tasnim Nisa is an aspiring writer who is committed to raising awareness about child sexual abuse, victim-blaming, and the need for stronger legal and social protections.

item.title: Who gets to be heard in Bangladesh?
item.description:
Imagine a river swallowing a neighbourhood in Manhattan. By noon, the world is outraged.
Now imagine the same river taking homes in Bangladesh every monsoon for decades. Barely a headline. Why?
Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak’s seminal essay, “Can the Subaltern Speak?” (1988), argues that the voices of the most marginalized populations, the “subaltern,” are silenced not by force but by the frameworks of intellectual discourse itself.
Originally a military term for lower-ranking officers, “subaltern” was adapted into social and political theory by Antonio Gramsci to describe subordinate classes living under the hegemony of ruling elites.
Historian Ranajit Guha later founded the Subaltern Studies collective to rewrite South Asian history from below.
Spivak engaged with that project as a critic, pushing the concept through a deconstructive lens.
Her conclusion is often misread. The subaltern is not literally unable to speak.
They cannot be heard or recognized on their own terms within dominant systems of knowledge.
While she used oppressed women as her example, the concept is not exclusive to them. It applies to anyone left unheard in colonial and postcolonial societies.
The danger lies with the well-meaning: when scholars speak for the subaltern, they may inadvertently reinforce colonial power structures and the colonial reading of the situation.
The relevance of subaltern theory in the socio-economic context of Bangladesh, a country born of colonial partition and postcolonial development struggles, finds clear resonance. Despite the country’s vibrant political culture, public dialogue and national discourse largely exist in two interconnected spheres: academic discourse and mainstream discourse.
Academic discourse is predominantly shaped by scholars, policymakers, and intellectual elites who debate questions such as whether the Constitution should be reformed or amended.
Mainstream discourse, meanwhile, is largely shaped by the urban middle and upper-middle classes, particularly journalists, political commentators, social media influencers, and online intellectuals who dominate Bangladesh’s digital public sphere.
While the rural poor, workers, indigenous peoples, and others have virtually no forum in which their own voices can shape the conversation.
Their voices are not necessarily absent because they have nothing to say, but because the structures through which public discourse operates rarely allow them to speak on their own terms.
Consider what daily life looks like for millions. It is defined not by constitutional debates or ideological disputes but by survival: the next meal, malnutrition, affordable healthcare, stable work, the squeeze of inflation.
Under such conditions, joining intellectual or political discourse is a privilege, not a practical possibility.
Many poor and rural Bangladeshis have limited formal education and civic literacy, so the legal and political language of these debates is unfamiliar.
Decision-makers and journalists tend to address “the people” in generic terms, turning individuals into statistics.
NGO and government reports might cite poverty data for a community but rarely include a single testimony from its members, in their own words. Attending policy forums or writing blog posts is a distant concern when the day is spent surviving.
As one study of rural women notes, although they may hear about development programs, their practical involvement is “tokenism,” invited to meetings only to satisfy formal requirements, while real decisions are made by others.
In short, their engagement is often “peripheral and performative,” not substantive.
This mirrors Spivak’s point that subalterns can speak, but the structures of power make it impossible for their voices to be heard or acted upon.
Major institutions remain concentrated in the hands of educated elites.
Policy and media debates, from national budget discussions to university syllabi, are shaped by those with formal power and influence, almost always from urban or upper-class backgrounds.
Grassroots leaders or community representatives have little access to these platforms. This reproduces a colonial-era pattern.
After independence in 1971 and before as well, Bangladesh’s elite retained much of the state machinery. As a result, even “progressive” policies are often debated in elite terms, side-lining the lived experience of the poorest. Because of these factors, public discussions in Bangladesh frequently occur about marginalised people, rather than with them.
Strikingly relevant is her insight that when well-meaning intellectuals or officials claim to speak for the subaltern, they often end up “ventriloquising” them, imposing elite interpretations on their lives instead of letting the subalterns speak for themselves. In the Bangladeshi context, this can be seen in instances where poor women or minority communities are represented only as case studies or footnotes.
Rather than just improving service delivery or hearing them in isolated surveys, policymakers must actively create spaces where subaltern people lead the discussion.
Such measures recognise Spivak’s warning that representation must mean letting subalterns define issues in their own terms. Subaltern theory suggests that giving marginalised Bangladeshis a real voice goes beyond formal quotas or token seats.
It calls for restructuring dialogue itself. Practical steps might include strengthening labor unions, farmers’ cooperatives, slum councils, indigenous community groups, etc., so they can develop their own leaders and agendas.
These bodies can articulate needs like land rights, safe housing, or local schools on their own terms.
Civic literacy programs in rural and urban slum areas could also help people understand how government and law work, and how to use their voice through village councils or local elections. Decision-makers, in turn, need to listen: policy forums on poverty alleviation or labor laws should include authentic community representatives.
Go back to the river. The families who lose their homes to it every monsoon have plenty to say. The question is whether anyone with power is prepared to listen.
Tasin Mahdi, a knowledge seeker who exhibits a profound commitment to the betterment of his home nation and a keen interest in international affairs.

item.title: Two killed in separate incidents in Dhaka
item.description:
A woman was killed after being hit by a bus in Dhaka’s Tikatuli on Monday, while a prison inmate died under treatment at Dhaka Medical College Hospital (DMCH) the same day.
The road accident occurred around 1:30pm beneath the Tikatuli foot overbridge. Police seized the bus involved in the accident and detained its driver.
Rina Rani Das, 40, was returning home on foot after dropping off her younger son, Prithu Raj Ghosh, 12, a sixth-grader at Nawabpur School, her elder son Pronoy Ghosh said.
As she was crossing the road beneath the foot overbridge, two buses operated by Bandhan Paribahan and Doel Paribahan were reportedly racing against each other. The Doel Paribahan bus hit Rina, throwing her onto the road and leaving her critically injured.
With police assistance, she was rescued and taken to the DMCH emergency department around 4:00pm. Doctors declared her dead after examination.
Sub-Inspector Abu Bakkar of Wari Police Station said Rina’s body had been kept at the DMCH morgue. Police had seized the bus and detained its driver in connection with the incident.
Rina was the wife of Biswajit Ghosh of Ibrahim village in Nabinagar upazila, Brahmanbaria. She worked as a domestic help and lived with her family on KM Das Lane in Tikatuli. She is survived by her husband and two sons.
Meanwhile, Akash Biswas, 24, an inmate of Dhaka Central Jail, died while receiving treatment at DMCH on Monday afternoon.
Jail authorities had directed prison guards to admit him to Ward 601 of the hospital’s medicine department on October 6 after he fell ill in custody.
He died around 3:30pm on Monday after undergoing medical examinations, while under treatment.
Inspector Md Habibur Rahman, in charge of the DMCH police outpost, confirmed the death, saying the body had been kept at the hospital morgue for an autopsy.
Akash was the son of Abdul Gafur Biswas of the Kotwali area in Jessore. The case in which he was detained was not immediately known.

item.title: Women make up 48.5% of textile workforce but lag in supervisory roles
item.description:
Women account for 48.5% of the workforce in 25 textile mills assessed in Bangladesh but remain underrepresented in wet processing and supervisory and managerial positions, according to a gender assessment presented at a national consultation in Dhaka on Monday.
The consultation on the Gender Action Plan in the Textile Sector was organized by the Environment and Social Development Organization (ESDO), in collaboration with the Department of Environment (DoE) and project partners, to strengthen gender-responsive chemical management and occupational health and safety in the industry.
Held under the project “Reducing Uses and Releases of Chemicals of Concern, Including Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs), in the Textiles Sector,” the event brought together government officials, technical experts and other stakeholders to discuss workplace risks and identify measures to improve chemical safety and women's participation in decision-making.
Speaking at the event, Regional Gender Expert Dr Khondaker Golam Moazzem said women accounted for 48.5% of the workforce across the 25 assessed textile mills but remained underrepresented in wet processing and supervisory and managerial roles.
He said gender-responsive chemical safety measures should address women's specific occupational risks, ensure equal access to safety training and appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE), and include women in workplace decision-making.
The consultation featured findings from the national gender assessment and a draft National Gender Action Plan (NGAP). Participants discussed gaps in chemical safety information, protective equipment, occupational health and safety training, reproductive health and sex-disaggregated data.
National Gender Expert Siddika Sultana said the assessment had identified shortcomings in gender-responsive risk assessments, PPE provision, safety training and reproductive health measures.
She said the draft action plan provides a framework with specific actions, defined responsibilities and measurable targets, but effective implementation would require shared ownership among government agencies, factory management and workers.
In his welcome address, Department of Environment Deputy Director and National Focal Point Kazi Suman said a regional project covering Bangladesh, Indonesia, Pakistan and Vietnam aimed to reduce hazardous chemical use in the textile industry.
The initiative includes preparing chemical inventories in 125 factories. Safer alternatives have so far been introduced in 2 factories, alongside capacity-building activities, he said.
National Project Coordinator Dr Mahfuzul Haque said Bangladesh's textile sector employed more than 3 million workers, many of whom were women. Workers were exposed to chemicals of concern and persistent organic pollutants, which studies have linked to reproductive health risks among both men and women, he added.
Dr Anton Purnomo, director of BCRC-SEA in Indonesia, said the project aimed to reach 10,000 direct beneficiaries across the region, 60% of whom would be women.
He outlined 3 priorities: gender-responsive occupational health and chemical safety, greater participation and opportunities for women, and sustainable interventions supported by measurable indicators and clear timelines.
Speaking as the chief guest, Dr Md Saidur Rahman, additional secretary at the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, said the Environment Conservation Rules 2023 set standards for 15 chemicals across 13 industrial sectors, including textile dyeing and washing.
He said the government wanted to work with industries to reduce chemical use rather than rely solely on enforcement.
He also urged the Department of Environment to ensure that textile factories operated both biological and chemical effluent treatment plants (ETPs), noting that wastewater from dyeing and washing continued to pollute the Turag, Shitalakkhya and Buriganga rivers.
ESDO Senior Technical Adviser Professor Dr Shahriar Hossain said gender considerations should be addressed through equity and justice rather than focusing exclusively on women, as the project covered all workers, employees and management personnel exposed to chemicals.
He said the initiative did not seek to eliminate chemicals altogether or identify per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) without laboratory testing. Instead, it assessed existing chemical use and piloted safer alternatives in selected factories to encourage a shift toward greener chemicals.
In his closing remarks, consultation moderator and Department of Environment Director Parvez Chowdhury said women accounted for nearly half of the textile workforce but remained underrepresented in chemical-intensive wet processing jobs.
“The solution is not to exclude women, but to make every workplace safe for them,” he said.
The consultation aimed to translate the gender assessment findings into a practical action plan with clear responsibilities, timelines, indicators and monitoring arrangements.
ESDO and its partners said the initiative sought to strengthen institutional accountability, improve women's access to safety measures and training, and promote their participation in occupational health and safety initiatives across Bangladesh's textile sector.

item.title: CUET vice-chancellor confined to office for nearly 15 hours
item.description:
Professor Sheikh Shariful Alam, vice-chancellor of Chittagong University of Engineering and Technology (CUET), has been confined to his office for nearly 15 hours.

Students demanding the reinstatement of former vice-chancellor Professor Abu Sadaat Muhammad Sayem locked the main gate of the administrative building at around 12:30 pm on Monday, trapping him inside. At a press conference in the evening, the protesters demanded the current vice-chancellor’s resignation.

At 3:00 am on Tuesday, as this report was being written, students were still gathered in front of the administrative building. At around 1:30 am, reports emerged that someone inside the building had fallen ill.

Md Abdullah, a physician at CUET’s medical centre, went to the building, accompanied by journalists who also entered.

Abdullah checked the blood pressure of an engineer named Shahriar. He said Shahriar’s systolic blood pressure was 170 mmHg and his diastolic pressure was 100 mmHg. He subsequently advised that Shahriar be taken to Chittagong Medical College Hospital. The physician said another person had also fallen ill but was not taken to hospital.

Asked about his health, Vice-Chancellor Sheikh Shariful Alam told Prothom Alo that he was well.

“Two of our alumni members are suffering from complications related to high blood pressure. So I called an ambulance and a physician. Since everyone here has been confined for a long time, they are feeling unwell and exhausted,” he added.

On 21 September, Professor Sheikh Shariful Alam, previously at Khulna University of Engineering and Technology (KUET), was appointed vice-chancellor of CUET. Students had already begun protesting the removal of Professor Abu Sadaat Muhammad Sayem and demanding his reinstatement.

Since 22 September, they have been enforcing a total shutdown. University teachers, officers and employees have also been observing a work stoppage in support of the same demand. As a result, classes, examinations and other academic activities have remained suspended for nearly three weeks.

The protesting students alleged that at around 9:00 am on Monday, the vice-chancellor broke the lock on the administrative building’s gate and entered his office accompanied by leaders and activists of the CUET unit of Jatiyatabadi Chhatra Dal, the BNP’s student wing.

After learning of his arrival, the students gave him until noon to leave the building. When he failed to do so, they locked the main gate at around 12:30 pm.

The vice-chancellor was joined inside the building by CUET Chhatra Dal unit president Wasif Rashed and his associates, as well as several current and former students. According to the latest information available, between 10 and 11 people, including the vice-chancellor, remained confined inside.

item.title: Will BNP activists think about these issues?
item.description:
Congratulations to the Bangladeshi nationalist activists and organisers.
As the organisational foundation of the government, you are a significant force in the country. Previously, your party has achieved a majority in elections at least four times. In the most recent election, the BNP received almost 50 per cent of the vote and over two hundred parliamentary seats. The present and future of the country now depend on your proper thinking and actions.

There is no alternative to relying on you for the comfort and prosperity of the citizens. This letter is a humble personal reflection. You are the guardian of all those who voted for you and those who did not. The party might belong to individuals, but the government belongs to everyone. At least, it should be, and it needs to be.

Even if experts may not want it, in this country, the government and party become synonymous—hence, you are the only post office for the citizens. Furthermore, the parliamentary system and its practice here are such that when a party secures more than 150 seats, the opposition becomes a paper tiger. At that point, whatever the government desires is affirmed with a ''yes'' or ''no'' in parliament. History indicates that the consequences of this are not favourable.

In the past, when the country was devoid of strong opposition or they couldn't play an effective role, the government faced difficulties, and the citizens suffered as well.

As former organisers of the ruling party, you are aware that the nature of bureaucracy in Bangladesh is such that they don't have the courage to inform about the field's real situation—they might not even want to. In such circumstances, the clamors from the opposition about various issues help the government understand the ground reality. This is how the opposition works to protect the government in a democracy. Our 'tradition' doesn't work that way. The repeated undignified and violent exits of governments are due to the lack of a strong and constructive opposition or not allowing the opposition to function effectively. We question whether we are facing such concerns again.

It is true that there is an electoral mandate for the BNP to govern the state alone. However, it is your responsibility to evaluate and reassess if the party's policymakers are making the right decisions. There is no effective route for the evaluations of a non-partisan civil society to reach the secretariat or national parliament. In this case, you need to demonstrate the courage of a constructive opposition.

In this country, political party decisions, preferences, and dislikes all come from the top. A small same group or faction makes national decisions in most cases. If decisions made in this way result in adverse outcomes, the party's workers, along with everyone else, fall into trouble.

In 2024, certainly, there wasn't much opportunity for the grass-root workers to express their opinions on the rulers' decisions. However, they are severely suffering from that governance culture now. No one knows when this suffering will end for them, although their leaders are not in bad shape in Europe-America. There are many lessons to be learned for the future.

The way to prevent such a situation from happening again is for the workers of the ruling party to continually express independent opinions. If there is a mistake in government work, prompt the policymakers to stop and, if possible, make them stop.

A dangerous political culture has already developed in Bangladesh—where workers have to bear catastrophic liability for the ruling party's decisions. Therefore, blindly supporting everything within the party would be suicidal. Surely no ruling party workers today or in the future will want to escape like the past ones of the ousted party. That's why putting the party leadership under accountability pressure is necessary. It has become a duty for political and social security reasons. History has brought us to such a new chapter.

It might sound harsh, but politicians have made politics extremely dangerous. So, for personal and family safety, political workers must have independent assessments of and express opinions about the upper echelon's actions. The main lesson of the post-Awami League era is that honest dissent offers more security than blind 'consensus'.

The BNP has secured over two hundred seats directly in the election. With reserved seats, you have a significant number of MPs. However, many unelected individuals are in critical roles in government administration. Many who have returned from abroad are also there. This isn't a new tradition in this country. If there is no long-term, close connection between the policy-makers and society, you can compensate for it as grassroots workers-organisers-associates. Because of your active involvement at the grassroots level, you know what actions need to be prioritised for the majority of people.

Does Bangladesh currently need dozens of Airbus and Boeing aircraft, or should investment in agriculture, poultry, and fisheries be increased—that is something you should understand best. You can convey these things to MPs and ministers. Convey your thoughts on these matters now in district and sub-district committee meetings.

Surely, you have observed that in various international indices, Bangladesh's position has recently declined significantly. Though the news might be small, they carry significant messages. This year, in the World Economic Forum''s Global Gender Gap Report, Bangladesh fell 55 places in one stroke. Women represent 90-100 million of our population. Their worsening situation means decreased prosperity for the entire country. This news does not align at all with the much-discussed 23rd clause of your '31-points'.

Last week, the World Bank reported that 62 million people are barely surviving near the poverty line—any economic issue could plunge them below it. An added concern is that the poverty rate has been increasing for four years in the country. The World Bank also states that in 2026, 2.1 million people have newly become poor.

Policy-makers in the country are surely aware of these reports from the world's top organisations. Opposition leaders might also be aware. Is there any reflection of this in parliamentary discussions and decisions?

According to the World Bank, substantial employment generation is necessary to reduce the current poverty rate and future concerning poverty fears in Bangladesh. However, in the past eight months, the government opened large expenditure accounts on metro rail, state employee salaries, and the purchase of aircraft. Do these match with the actual grassroots priorities? As workers of the ruling party past, present, and future, we will ask these questions from you!

37. 6 million people voted for you. Among them, how many are state employees, and how many are unemployed youth, workers, and farmers? You will undoubtedly analyze that.

I also present for your considerate evaluation, if everything from railways to ports has to be operated by foreign and private sectors, then why should the nation bear the costs of such a large cabinet and advisory board? Although there was mention of a small cabinet at the start, it has already crossed 50 members.

There are many advisors and special assistants as well. In Nepal, following a mass uprising, one of the first steps the government took was to reduce the number of ministries to 18. Alongside reducing revenue expenditure, it brought additional speed to the administrative decision-making process.

If not on these matters, at least reconsider laws like the Prevention of Enforced Disappearance Act, Human Rights Act, or potential Cyber Security Act? These laws will remain even with a change in power! Just as the RAB created by your past government remained in subsequent regimes and you experienced its ramifications.

We know that wise people learn from the past while the knowledgeable learn from others' mistakes. We have 55 years of experience behind us. We have the recent past of the freshly ousted and 170 million hopefuls for a bright future. It's all in your hands. Best wishes.

#Altaf Parvez is researcher and writer

item.title: Saudi flight disruptions: CAAB issues 7 directives to assist affected passengers
item.description:
The Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh (CAAB) has issued seven directives to airlines to ease the difficulties faced by passengers affected by flight disruptions at various airports following attacks by Houthi rebels in Saudi Arabia.

The directives call for airlines to provide the latest flight information, assist passengers with rebooking and refunds, and ensure essential services for those stranded at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka.

The instructions were issued in a letter signed on Monday night by Group Captain SM Ragib Samad, executive director of Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, and sent to the airlines concerned.

Fresh blow to overseas employment in Saudi Arabia

The letter states that operations at various airports in Saudi Arabia have been significantly disrupted by the country’s current security situation. All airlines operating direct and transit flights to Saudi Arabia must implement the directives immediately.

Under the directives, passengers must be informed of flight cancellations, delays and schedule changes through various channels, including text messages, phone calls, emails, websites and social media.

Airlines must also provide clear information about revised schedules, rebooking, refunds and other applicable arrangements. Passengers must be advised not to come to the airport until their flight status has been confirmed, it stated.

Airlines must advise passengers who need visa extensions or immigration-related assistance to contact the Saudi authorities, the Saudi Embassy in Dhaka and other relevant agencies.

The directives also require airlines to ensure essential services including seating, drinking water and light refreshments for passengers who have already arrived at the airport. Special attention must be given to elderly people, children, persons with disabilities and other vulnerable passengers.

In addition, each airline must appoint a designated representative and promptly provide the Flight Management Department at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport with their name, designation, mobile phone number and email address.

Until the situation returns to normal, the representative must remain in contact with the airport authorities to assist passengers and coordinate flight-related information, as per the directives.

CAAB further stated that no passenger should be left stranded without assistance. Airlines must treat passengers with empathy and provide accurate and complete information. The directives must be implemented immediately, with airlines maintaining coordination with the airport’s Flight Management Department.

51 flights cancelled or suspended from Dhaka, 5,418 passengers affected

Saudi flight situation

Disruptions at various airports in Saudi Arabia have affected 62 flights operating from Bangladesh on direct and transit routes, leaving 9,674 passengers affected.

According to CAAB, these figures, based on information available up to Monday afternoon, do not include passengers travelling with Riyadh Air.

CAAB’s figures show that, among direct flights, nine operated by Biman Bangladesh Airlines, two by US-Bangla Airlines, five by Saudia and seven by Riyadh Air have been affected. In addition, 39 transit flights operated by IndiGo, Emirates, Qatar Airways, flydubai, SalamAir and EgyptAir have also been affected.

Meanwhile, Biman Bangladesh Airlines has suspended all flights on the Dhaka–Riyadh route until 17 October. US-Bangla Airlines has also cancelled all flights on the Dhaka–Riyadh–Dhaka route until 21 October.

item.title: Bangladesh need four wickets in a gripping final session
item.description:
The Abu Dhabi Test is going down to the wire, with Bangladesh needing four wickets and Afghanistan requiring 214 runs to win in the final session of the fifth and final day.

Afghanistan reached 264-6 in 106 overs at tea, with opener Sedikullah Atal unbeaten on 100 and captain Hashmatullah Shahidi dismissed for 36 shortly before the break.

Shahidi fell attempting a big shot off Mehidy Hasan Miraz, giving Hasan Mahmud a catch at mid-on. The wicket gave Bangladesh a crucial breakthrough after Afghanistan had fought hard to keep the match alive.

Litton Das sets world record

Atal, meanwhile, has produced a remarkable rearguard innings, reaching his maiden Test and first-class century off 277 balls. He has been central to Afghanistan’s resistance as they try to save the match while keeping their hopes of a victory alive.

Bangladesh had earlier removed Ismat Alam for four off 60 balls, with Miraz taking the wicket, but Atal’s century has kept Afghanistan in contention.

With one session remaining, the Test has become a compelling contest between Bangladesh’s bowlers and Afghanistan’s stubborn resistance — a reminder of the drama that makes Test cricket special.

item.title: Harassing Prof Yunus has exposed the character of Awami League: Nahid Islam
item.description:
Nahid Islam, Chief Whip of the Opposition in the National Parliament and convener of the National Citizen Party (NCP), has strongly condemned and protested the incident in which Professor Muhammad Yunus, former chief adviser of the interim government, was harassed at a US airport.

He said the attempt to harass Professor Yunus at John F Kennedy International Airport in the United States has once again exposed the brutal, violent, and inhuman nature of Awami League’s (whose activities are banned) terror-dependent politics.

Nahid Islam made these remarks in a statement sent to the media today, Tuesday.

A video of the incident, in which Professor Yunus was harassed as he left New York’s airport in a wheelchair last Monday, has circulated on social media. The video shows several people approaching Professor Yunus and shouting slogans at him in loud voices.

At the time, the protesters were shouting various accusatory and insulting remarks directed at him, including “Why did you come here?” and “Go back.” Several expatriate supporters of Awami League, whose activities are banned, have been accused of harassing him.

Nahid Islam described the incident as an “attempt by fascist terrorists” and said that even two years after being decisively rejected by the people of Bangladesh, there has been not the slightest change in the character of the Awami League’s terrorist forces. There is not even the slightest sign of remorse among them for their past misdeeds.

“This terrorist network, active both at home and abroad, must be completely thwarted. The trials of those involved in enforced disappearances and killings during the fascist era, including the July massacre, must be completed and the verdicts swiftly implemented. In addition, the trial of the Awami League as a political party must begin immediately on charges of genocide and terrorism,” he said.

In the statement, NCP convener Nahid Islam further said that, at a critical juncture in the nation’s history, members of the interim government, including Professor Yunus, had taken the helm of the country and led efforts to restore democracy and rebuild an economy reduced to ruins.
He said the government must take effective measures to ensure the security of all of them.

Meanwhile, Zahed Ur Rahman, the Prime Minister’s adviser on information and broadcasting, said legal action would be taken over the harassment of Professor Muhammad Yunus in the United States.

Responding to a journalist’s question at the government’s regular press briefing at the Secretariat today, Tuesday, where the government’s activities were discussed, he said that the same legal measures taken after actress Azmeri Haque Badhon was harassed in Italy would also be pursued in this case.

item.title: Illusion of independence: Why Bangladesh Bank needs market instruments, not just legal autonomy
item.description:
Whenever systemic distress in Bangladesh’s banking sector surfaces, "central bank independence" is invoked as the sovereign remedy. Strip the Ministry of Finance of its informal veto, insulate Bangladesh Bank from executive directives and institutional discipline—we are told—will return.
Yet this diagnosis confuses legal autonomy with operational capacity.

Central bank independence is not merely a statutory shield inscribed in an amended Bangladesh Bank Order; it is an institutional technology. When a monetary authority lacks market-clearing transmission tools and non-discretionary supervisory mechanisms, even an ostensibly autonomous regulator is forced to govern by administrative decree. In finance, administrative discretion is the primary currency of cronyism.

To understand why autonomy has repeatedly unraveled, we must first ask: independence from whom?

Conventional macroeconomic theory fixates on fiscal dominance—preventing elected governments from printing money to finance deficit spending ahead of elections. In Bangladesh, however, the far deadlier capture has been commercial. Over recent decades, concentrated conglomerates colonised commercial bank boards and captured the regulatory perimeter.

Ordinary depositors are widely dispersed, unorganised, and possess zero lobbying power. Chronic delinquent borrowers, by contrast, are concentrated, highly capitalised, and politically entrenched. A central bank’s essential mandate is to act as the fiduciary guardian of public savings against the insatiable appetites of concentrated capital. When that independence fails, depositors bear the quiet tax of negative real yields, currency misalignments, and systemic bailouts.

Why was Bangladesh Bank structurally unable to defend this perimeter? Because it suffered from an acute dual instrument deficit across both monetary policy transmission and banking supervision.

True autonomy will arrive not when a governor is granted absolute personal discretion, but when the central bank is equipped with the market instruments to govern impersonally, and bound by statutory rules to let the consequences fall where they may.

The monetary impasse: Governing without markets

In a functioning architecture, a central bank steers the macroeconomy impersonally. It adjusts its policy rate, which transmits through an active interbank market, anchors a competitive yield curve across liquid secondary government debt, and prices commercial credit and deposits.

The foreign exchange market clears based on external supply and demand. In Bangladesh, these mechanisms were systematically suppressed:

• Absence of a Secondary Debt Market: Government securities remained a captive, buy-and-hold space dominated by statutory reserve requirements rather than active trading. Primary Treasury auctions were routinely subjected to yield caps and direct devolvement onto Bangladesh Bank's balance sheet, destroying yield-curve discovery and rendering Open Market Operations (OMO) toothless.

• Managed Exchange Rate Distortions: Rather than allowing market-clearing price discovery, the central bank maintained an artificially defended exchange rate. When external balances deteriorated, authorities resorted to fragmented administrative rates, moral suasion on Authorized Dealer banks, and import-letter-of-credit rationing. This depleted foreign exchange reserves, fueled wide curb-market premiums, and delayed macro adjustments.

• Administrative Rate Ceilings: To suppress borrowing costs by fiat, the central bank enforced rigid 9% lending and 6% deposit caps. This severed the link between monetary policy rates and commercial bank pricing, penalised savers with negative real returns, and subsidized corporate leverage while inflation accelerated.

The supervisory collapse: Discretion over rules

This reliance on administrative fiat in monetary policy mirrored an identical failure in bank supervision. In mature jurisdictions, supervisors rely on automated Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) frameworks and statutory resolution tools. When capital or asset quality deteriorates past statutory thresholds, mandatory sanctions trigger by law: dividends are halted, balance-sheet expansion is frozen, and non-viable management is removed without political negotiation.

Crucially, an effective PCA regime relies on timely, honest provisioning. In Bangladesh, banks systematically fail to make adequate or timely provisions, aided by external auditors who rubber-stamp cosmetic balance sheets. Because Bangladesh Bank lacks automated supervisory tools to detect and penalise balance-sheet misrepresentation in real time, profound information asymmetry is created. Depositors and investors are kept in the dark, believing distressed institutions are well-capitalised until capital deficits become catastrophic.

Deprived of objective, automated tools, the central bank substituted supervision with administrative circulars:

• Instead of enforcing non-discretionary provisioning and Basel III deductions, it issued ad-hoc circulars that repeatedly relaxed loan classification criteria to conceal bad debt.

• Instead of forcing credit recognition, it permitted repeat defaulters to regularize massive bad debts through nominal 2% down payments and multi-year rescheduling windows.

• When distressed assets choked interbank liquidity, the central bank quietly deployed emergency liquidity lifelines to keep zombie lenders alive.
The result of this supervisory vacuum is the catastrophe of Non-Performing Loans (NPLs). Today, bad loans represent a massive share of the banking sector's balance sheet, with total distressed assets exceeding Tk 600,000 crore and several captured institutions completely decapitalised.

The pathology of discretion

The lesson across both mandates is identical: administrative measures are never a systemic substitute for market instruments.

A market-determined Treasury yield, a floating exchange rate, or an automated PCA trigger is impersonal—blind to borrower identity, bank ownership, or political clout. An administrative decree, by contrast, requires an official’s signature.

The moment monetary transmission and supervisory enforcement hinge on a signature—whether granting an LC quota, fixing a rate cap, or approving an ad-hoc loan-rescheduling circular—that signature becomes a prize to be lobbied for, pressured, or bought. Administrative discretion did not resolve market frictions; it created a lucrative marketplace for regulatory forbearance, the evergreening of bad debt, and policy capture.

Housing both mandates under one roof without statutory separation worsened this: central bank liquidity was repeatedly deployed to prop up failing banks under its supervisory watch, compromising price stability to conceal supervisory failure.

Restoring functional autonomy

If Bangladesh Bank is to escape this trap, reform must focus on operational instruments rather than legal platitudes:

1. Build Secondary Sovereign Debt Markets: End Treasury bill devolvement onto the central bank. Establish genuine auction discovery and secondary liquidity so the policy repo rate transmits across an authentic yield curve.

2. Transition to Market-Clearing Exchange Rates: Eliminate administrative rationing in foreign exchange pricing, letting an authentic market rate clear external balances and protect reserves.

3. Statutory PCA with Automated Provisioning Triggers: Enact legally binding Prompt Corrective Action legislation where asset impairment and provisioning shortfalls trigger mandatory restrictions automatically. Integrate automated supervisory audit systems to penalise misrepresentation by banks and their external auditors, eliminating information asymmetry.

4. End the Bureaucratic Duopoly: Dismantle the Financial Institutions Division’s administrative oversight over state banks, establishing a single supervisory standard for all deposit-taking institutions.

5. Establish a Modern Resolution Architecture: Equip the central bank with statutory resolution powers to haircut wholesale creditors, wind down insolvent lenders, and transfer viable deposits to bridge institutions without judicial delays.

Central bank independence cannot survive as an abstract legal virtue. As long as Bangladesh Bank lacks secondary debt markets, flexible pricing channels, and automated resolution tools, it will remain hooked on administrative discretion—and wherever discretion reigns, capture will follow.

True autonomy will arrive not when a governor is granted absolute personal discretion, but when the central bank is equipped with the market instruments to govern impersonally, and bound by statutory rules to let the consequences fall where they may.

*Sajed ul Islam is a senior banking executive and financial markets specialist with three decades of global institutional experience across treasury, capital markets, and corporate governance.

item.title: Litton Das sets world record
item.description:
Ebadot Hossain’s bouncer brushed the gloves of Ikram Alikhil. Litton Das’s diving catch to his right was one to remember.

It was not just this catch, but Litton’s performance with both bat and with gloves behind the wicket in the Abu Dhabi Test will stay in the minds of spectators for a long time. It will also go down in the record books. With that catch, Litton set a world record.

The catch to dismiss Ikram, taken towards the end of the morning session on the fifth day of the Test today, Tuesday, was Litton’s ninth dismissal as a wicketkeeper in the match. Litton scored 53 in Bangladesh’s first innings and followed it with a 102 in the second.

Hasan Mahmud becomes first Bangladesh pacer to record Test hat-trick

Litton became the first wicketkeeper in Test history to score 50-plus runs in both innings and record nine dismissals in the same match. The previous record belonged to South Africa’s Denis Lindsay.

In the Johannesburg Test against Australia in 1966, Lindsay scored 50-plus runs in both innings and recorded eight dismissals. By catching Ikram, Litton surpassed Lindsay to set a new record.

The record for the most dismissals by a wicketkeeper in a single Test match is now within Litton’s reach.

England’s Jack Russell, South Africa’s AB de Villiers and India’s Rishabh Pant currently share the record, with 11 dismissals each in a match. Litton needs two more dismissals to equal their record and three to break it.

Bangladesh declare after Litton’s century, set Afghanistan 479 to win

Former England wicketkeeper Russell recorded 11 dismissals against South Africa in a Test in Johannesburg in 1995.

Eighteen years later, at the same venue, South African legend de Villiers equalled Russell’s record in a Test against Pakistan. Pant joined them by recording 11 dismissals against Australia in the Adelaide Test in 2018.

Wicketkeepers have recorded nine dismissals in a single Test match 31 times, including today. There have been five instances of 10 dismissals.

As of yesterday, Litton had already set the Bangladesh record for the most dismissals by a wicketkeeper in a single Test, with eight. The previous record belonged to Khaled Mashud, who recorded seven dismissals against Zimbabwe in 2004.

item.title: Dalit women seek security to contest elections
item.description:
“There are 1,800 Dalit votes in my area. I have the courage to contest an election, but I do not feel safe.” Sonamoni Modak, a Dalit woman living in Keraniganj, Dhaka, made this remark as she expressed her interest in contesting a reserved seat for women in a future local government election.

According to her, when Dalit women express an interest in contesting elections, influential candidates in their areas intimidate them by asking, “Do you really think you can do it?”

Sathi Sarkar, another Dalit woman from the same area, echoed her views, saying that no Dalit woman would be able to contest an election without assurances of security and support.

At a roundtable discussion held at the Prothom Alo office in Karwan Bazar, Dhaka, on Sunday, the invited Dalit women described the obstacles they face when attempting to become election candidates.

Three other Dalit women, Lipi Sarkar, Tithi Mondol and Shampa Rani Das said that insecurity, a lack of support from political parties, family opposition and derogatory remarks from society often prevent them from contesting elections.

The non-governmental development organisation, Avijan and Prothom Alo organised the roundtable under the title “Dalit women’s rights in local politics: Challenges and the way forward”.

The Government of Sweden supported the event, while the International Foundation for Electoral Systems (IFES) provided technical assistance.

The keynote paper presented at the discussion estimated that Bangladesh has between 5.5 million (55 lakh) and 6.5 million (65 lakh) people from Dalit communities.

Divided into more than 50 communities, these people face discrimination based on their ancestry and occupations. Dalit women experience even greater discrimination.

Although they can register as voters, they have limited opportunities to become elected representatives.

The paper recommended that Dalit organisations, non-governmental organisations and political parties initiate dialogue among Dalit voters and communities in areas with relatively high numbers of Dalit voters before future local government elections.

Such initiatives could encourage communities to support a single candidate and prevent votes from being split. Families should also support Dalit women who wish to contest elections rather than dismiss their candidacies as a source of trouble.

Prime Minister’s Political Adviser Zahir Uddin Swapon said the government was working to build an inclusive society and political system.

“We need to find ways to integrate Dalit people into this system. We must make the government aware of what Dalit women and men want. The responsibility of Dalit communities is to put forward their needs and expectations as demands within the initiatives the government has announced,” he said.

Prime Minister’s Special Assistant Bijon Kanti Sarkar said local government elections had not been fair in the past because of the actions of a particular political party. He added that the government had so far decided that local government elections would not be held on a party basis.

“There is no legal barrier. Dalit women will be able to participate in elections without fear,” he said. In his view, nobody would simply hand people their rights. “People have to claim their rights and earn respect,” he added.

Three BNP women MPs speak at the discussion

Three women MPs from the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), representing reserved seats for women in the Jatiya Sangsad, spoke at the event.

Newaz Halima Arly said people must not use disadvantaged Dalit women merely as a vote bank. Madhabi Marma said, opportunities should be given to the Dalit women to contest local government elections based on population in their respective areas.

She also added that, changing patriarchal attitudes is also much needed. Fahmida Haque said collective efforts could help Dalit women make progress.

Rumana Amin, the country representative of the International Foundation for Electoral Systems (IFES), said stakeholders must determine the steps needed to remove the barriers that Dalit women face in local government elections.

Mohammed Zakaria, director general of the NGO Affairs Bureau, said his organisation would support Dalit women whenever they needed assistance.

Subrata Chowdhury, acting president of Gano Forum, urged Dalit communities to organise themselves. “You cannot sit back and depend on the generosity of others. You must organise yourselves. You must continue to fight for your rights in every sphere,” he said.

Banani Biswas, executive director of Avijan, called for the enactment of an anti-discrimination law. Urging authorities to create opportunities for Dalit women to participate in local government elections, she said, “There are many villages where Dalit women would win if they stood as candidates. However, various pressures prevent them from finding the courage to contest.”

Manindra Kumar Nath, acting general secretary of the Bangladesh Hindu Buddhist Christian Unity Council, said Dalit women could make progress in politics if political parties showed genuine commitment.

Fauzia Moslem, president of the Bangladesh Mahila Parishad, said politics had become the centre of power. “Therefore, we must be part of this centre of power if we want to realise our demands. Dalit women must have the opportunity not only to vote but also to get elected,” she said.

Ruhin Hossain Prince, former general secretary of the Communist Party of Bangladesh, said authorities must first ensure that Dalit women could meet their basic needs, including education, healthcare and housing. He also added that it is important to integrate them into mainstream society while ensuring the development of their own culture.

Urging Dalit women to overcome their inferiority complex and come forward, Luva Nahid Choudhury, director general of the Bengal Foundation, said society and the state create conditions that lead to deprivation. Arts and culture could challenge these entrenched perceptions.

Other speakers included Anik Asad, country director of Muslim Hands UK; Moriam Nessa, lead for women’s rights and gender equality at ActionAid Bangladesh; Shourza Talukder, senior research associate at the Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD); Prodip Haldar, head of the Department of Sociology at Government Ispahani Degree College; Syeda Samara Mortada, partnership analyst at UN Women Bangladesh; and Manisha Biswas, legal specialist at the Bangladesh Legal Aid and Services Trust (BLAST).

Jannat-e-Ferdousi Lucky, general secretary of the Research and Development Collective (RDC), presented the keynote paper, while Jayanti Roy, vice-president of Avijan, delivered the vote of thanks.

Firoz Choudhury, assistant editor of Prothom Alo, moderated the discussion.

item.title: “I ordered 200 cylinders, but the company supplied only 50”
item.description:
“I ordered 200 cylinders for today, but the company supplied only 50. Meanwhile, my customers keep calling one after another. How can I explain the shortage to them?”

Rabiul Islam, an LPG cylinder seller near Mohammadpur bus stand in the capital, said this when he spoke to Prothom Alo at around 10am on Tuesday.

Rabiul said the shortage of LPG cylinders had persisted for several days. Demand had increased further since Monday, he added.

Nahid Islam, owner of Dipu Enterprise in the Shankar area of Dhanmondi, reported a similar shortage. “My daily demand is 70 to 80 cylinders, but today I received only 20. So many people are calling, but I can’t take their orders,” he said.

Prothom Alo visited shops selling LPG cylinders in Adabar, Mohammadpur, Dhanmondi, Farmgate and Karwan Bazar in the capital and spoke to shop owners and employees, who described the same situation. Customers were calling to order cylinders, while others were coming to the shops in person only to leave empty-handed. Some were managing to buy cylinders, but others were going away without any.

Mohammad Hedayetullah, a seller in Farmgate, said he was supplying cylinders to customers who had already placed orders and taking new orders for delivery when fresh supplies arrived.

On 4 October, the Bangladesh Energy Regulatory Commission (BERC) announced a new LPG price for the domestic market, raising the price of a 12kg cylinder by Tk 252 to Tk 1,837.

However, visits to various parts of the capital on Tuesday found that customers were having to pay an additional Tk 400–450 for each 12kg LPG cylinder. Shops were selling the cylinders for Tk 2,200 to Tk 2,250 each.

Bismillah Enterprise in the Tikkapara area of Mohammadpur had one 45kg cylinder available, priced at Tk 6,300. The shop was selling 12kg cylinders for Tk 2,200 and 5kg cylinders, including the cylinder itself, for Tk 1,800.

Sagar Hossain, an employee at the shop, said, “We have orders for 40 cylinders of 12kg each today, but a delivery truck arrived with only 20. So many people are calling that we can’t supply everyone.”

On Monday, the LPG Traders Cooperative Society Limited announced that its members would close their shops nationwide on Thursday and Friday. The announcement came in support of several demands, including an end to the alleged harassment of LPG traders. The traders also warned that they could announce tougher action if their demands were not met.

The announcement has raised concerns among consumers.

On Tuesday morning, Prothom Alo spoke to a customer named Raisul Islam in Dhanmondi. He had come to buy a 12kg cylinder from Dipu Enterprise. Raisul sells tea from a roadside footpath stall in the Shankar area.

He said the gas remaining in his current cylinder would last another two or three days. However, having heard that cylinder sales would be suspended for two days, he had decided to buy one in advance. If he could not get gas, he would have to shut down his stall.

item.title: CUET protests: Some in government see political links, students disagree
item.description:
A stalemate has persisted for 22 days at Chittagong University of Engineering and Technology (CUET) over protests demanding the reinstatement of former vice-chancellor (VC) Professor Abu Sadat Muhammad Sayem.

Meanwhile, yesterday, Monday, 21 days after his appointment, the new vice-chancellor, Professor Sheikh Shariful Alam, entered the university accompanied by Jatiyatabadi Chhatra Dal (JCD) leaders.

As of 10:30 am today, Tuesday, when this report was being written, protesting students were keeping him confined. Students say they will not call off their protests until the new VC resigns and the former VC is reinstated. Overall, the situation has become increasingly complicated.

Amid the circumstances, the government’s lack of any visible initiative to resolve the university’s crisis has raised questions. Some at the government’s policymaking level believe there may be political involvement behind the protests.

CUET vice-chancellor confined for over 23 hours

Some policymakers also believe politics was behind the protests over the appointment of a new VC at Dhaka University of Engineering and Technology (DUET) in Gazipur last May, as well as the movement against the VC at Khulna University of Engineering and Technology (KUET) during the interim government.

The protesting students at CUET, however, say their movement has no connection with party politics. They say they are protesting with the university’s academic environment and students’ interests in mind. According to them, students have joined the movement spontaneously.

Several sources at CUET claim that rivalries among local leaders of the ruling party in Chattogram may have influenced the appointment and replacement of the VC. There is also discussion on campus that the change in the VC post was driven by the leaders’ preferences.

In addition, the decision to appoint a teacher from another university as the VC instead of someone from CUET’s own faculty has also prompted reactions among a section of the teachers and students.

Professor Abu Sadat Muhammad Sayem of CUET’s Department of Mechanical Engineering was appointed VC by the BNP government on 27 July. Just 56 days after he took office, he was relieved of his duties on 21 September, and Professor Sheikh Shariful Alam of Khulna University of Engineering and Technology (KUET) was appointed as the new VC.

Students began protesting that night in response to the decision and locked the VC’s residence. A complete shutdown began the following day, 22 September. Teachers, officers and employees also started a work stoppage with the same demand. As a result, classes and examinations at the university have remained suspended for more than three weeks.

CUET students lock building with vice-chancellor inside, chant ‘reject new VC’

To find out what steps the government was taking to resolve the situation, Prothom Alo spoke to a person involved in government policymaking. The policymaker said that a university vice-chancellor’s position was an administrative one and that the government would consider who would be best suited to run the university.

Students could protest over problems in classrooms or other education-related issues. However, the policymaker believed it was not appropriate for the students to protest against the decision of a vice-chancellor’s appointment.

The person added that they believed the CUET protests might have political links. In his view, the protests over the appointment of vice-chancellors at Khulna University of Engineering and Technology and, Dhaka University of Engineering and Technology also had political connections.

However, a student involved in the protests told Prothom Alo Tuesday morning that their movement had no connection with party politics. The protest was aimed at protecting the university’s academic environment and students’ interests, the student said.

According to the student, if party politics were involved, only one group of students would have taken part. Instead, students were participating in the movement spontaneously. Under the current circumstances, the student sees the reinstatement of former vice-chancellor Professor Abu Sadat Muhammad Sayem as the solution.

People associated with CUET say it is concerning that an institution of higher education has remained paralysed for days on end. This is affecting students’ studies and academic lives, while also disrupting the university’s normal operations. In their view, the government should take prompt and effective action to resolve the stalemate rather than allow the crisis to drag on.

A CUET student told Prothom Alo that they, too, wanted to return to classes. If the stalemate continued, there was a risk of session backlogs, the student said. They therefore wanted the prime minister to intervene to resolve the crisis.

item.title: 14 whistling teals return to nature
item.description:
Poultry trader Mohammad Rafiqul had bought whistling teals (pati sorali hansh) from a village and was carrying them around to sell in the city when he caught the attention of certain bird lovers. Members of the Nature and Wildlife Conservation Community, a voluntary organisation that has long worked to protect the environment and wildlife in Pabna, informed him about the relevant laws.

He promised never to buy or sell wild birds again and agreed to release the teals, also known as lesser whistling ducks. They took him to the lake on the campus of Pabna University of Science and Technology, where they released the ducks. Exhausted and weak, the ducks splashed about in the lake for a while before closing their eyes to rest. As evening fell, they took flight together in search of a safe place to shelter. This photo story captures the release of these 14 teals.

item.title: Two WhatsApp groups: What’s behind Debashish, Gulshan Ara’s arrests?
item.description:
Following the arrest of two retired military officers, police have alleged that they used two WhatsApp groups to raise funds and circulate provocative content. They have also been accused of using platforms for retired military officers to maintain contact with Awami League leaders.

Lieutenant Colonel (retired) Bijoy Debashish Narayan Paul, 47, and Lieutenant (retired) Kazi Gulshan Ara, 43, were arrested on allegations of conspiring to destabilise the country through these activities. The Dhaka Metropolitan Police’s Detective Branch (DB) arrested them during raids in the capital’s Pallabi and Banani DOHS areas late on Sunday night.

Officers involved in the operation, and a review of the first information report (FIR) and the police remand application submitted to the court, point to several allegations behind the arrests. These primarily concern anti-government propaganda, financing, political contacts and organised activities.

On Monday afternoon, police produced the two officers before a court and sought seven days’ remand. The remand application repeated similar allegations against them. After hearing both sides, Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Didarul Alam granted four days’ remand.

Officials familiar with the investigation said the two retired officers had been under intelligence surveillance for a long time. They alleged that the officers had been active on behalf of the Awami League (whose activities have been banned in the country).

Investigators also claimed to have found links between them and “spies” at home and abroad. These allegations were among the reasons for deciding to arrest them.

Investigators claim these platforms were used to maintain contact with former army chief General (retd) Aziz Ahmed, a former home minister and fugitive senior leaders of Awami League (whose activities have been banned in the country).

The case was filed with Pallabi police station in Dhaka, naming another 101 people as unidentified accused.

Allegations centred on 2 WhatsApp groups

DB sources said the two arrested officers and their associates were connected to two WhatsApp groups named ‘Bangladesh Awami League Supporters Alpha Number # 1’ and ‘BBM Transparency’.

Police allege that Debashish and Gulshan Ara used the groups to raise funds for anti-government activities. They are also accused of producing digital content intended to incite violence and circulating it on various social media platforms.

Two other platforms formed by retired military officers, ‘Unity Care’ and ‘Public Parliament’, have also been mentioned in the allegations.

Investigators claim these platforms were used to maintain contact with former army chief General (retd) Aziz Ahmed, a former home minister and fugitive senior leaders of Awami League (whose activities have been banned in the country).

The alleged objective was to rehabilitate the Awami League politically and organise activities against the state.

Facebook page and online propaganda

Sources familiar with the investigation said social media activity was another important factor behind the arrests. The police remand application alleges that content intended to incite violence and instability was produced and circulated through a Facebook page named ‘KalAjkal.com’.

Charges brought against 2 former army officers, put on 4-day remand

The application also cites a Facebook account said to belong to Kazi Gulshan Ara, accusing her of using it to disseminate propaganda against the state.

Police allege that, since 5 August 2024, the two arrested officers and their associates had engaged in conspiratorial and defamatory campaigns against the government and Bangladesh. They have also been accused of maintaining contact with individuals at home and abroad.

Why the 2018 Gonobhaban episode has resurfaced

The remand application refers to an incident in 2018 concerning the political contacts of the two retired officers.

It alleges that, on 27 November 2018, ahead of the national election, Kazi Gulshan Ara visited Gonobhaban with more than 150 retired military officers to express solidarity with and allegiance to then prime minister Sheikh Hasina.

The visit by retired military officers to Gonobhaban to declare their support for Hasina was reported in the media at the time.

Police further allege that a committee named ‘Bangabandhu Sena Parishad’ was subsequently formed with 101 associates. The two arrested officers have been accused of being involved in the organisation’s activities.

The remand application accuses the organisation of attempting to spread hatred among people from different professions and social groups, provoking riots and creating disorder.

It also alleges that its members expressed hatred and contempt towards the government through social media and appearances on various talk shows.

101 more accused; police seek information on 5 fronts

Besides Debashish and Gulshan Ara, 101 unidentified people have been named as accused in the case filed with Pallabi police station. The case was lodged by Mohammad Ali Akbar, a police inspector with the DB’s Pallabi zonal team.

The case cited various provisions of the Penal Code, the Anti-Terrorism Act and the Cyber Security Ordinance.

In the remand application submitted to the court, the investigating officer identified five areas in which further information was needed: establishing the identities and whereabouts of the other accused; identifying domestic and foreign “spies” involved in activities against the state; collecting digital evidence; identifying other websites and pages used on social media; and uncovering the underlying facts of the case.

The application also refers to investigating the sources of alleged illegal funding. Police say the two accused need to be questioned to obtain detailed information and establish whether others were involved.

Accused deny allegations in court

During the remand hearing, lawyers for the two retired military officers challenged the allegations made by police.

Mohammad Mashiur Rahman, counsel for Gulshan Ara, said she had been accused of attempting to destabilise the country through an appearance on a talk show. However, he argued, the application did not specify what she had said that could have destabilised the country or identified any concrete evidence against her.

Abdullah Al Mansur, counsel for Debashish, described the allegations against his client as unacceptable. Although a charge of sedition had been brought, he said, the remand application did not explain the basis for the allegation or specify what offence his client had committed.

State prosecutor Harun Or Rashid, meanwhile, said the accused had maintained regular contact with leaders and activists of the ousted government with the aim of destabilising the country. He also alleged that they had links with domestic and foreign spies.

Further information about the accused and their activities could be obtained through remand, he told the court.
